blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights a key challenge in storage systems: maintaining consistent low-latency responses for foreground tasks (e.g., user requests in databases like Redis or PostgreSQL) when mixed with background tasks (e.g., checkpointing or garbage collection). The paper introduces Request-centric I/O prioritization (RCP), which addresses priority inversions across the entire storage stack (caching, file system, block, and device layers). Unlike prior approaches, RCP tracks I/O criticality end-to-end, tagging requests as critical or non-critical and dynamically adjusting priorities to prevent low-priority background I/O from blocking high-priority foreground tasks. The authors demonstrate significant performance gains: up to 53% higher throughput and 42x better 99th-percentile latency in tests with PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis. The solution requires minimal application changes (e.g., 2 lines of code for Redis) and addresses both task and I/O dependency-induced priority inversions.
paper_title: Enlightening the I/O Path: A Holistic Approach for Application Performance
paper_abstract: In data-intensive applications, such as databases and keyvalue stores, reducing the request handling latency is important for providing better data services. In such applications, I/O-intensive background tasks, such as checkpointing, are the major culprit in worsening the latency due to the contention in shared I/O stack and storage. To minimize the contention, properly prioritizing I/Os is crucial but the effectiveness of existing approaches is limited for two reasons. First, statically deciding the priority of an I/O is insufficient since high-priority tasks can wait for low-priority I/Os due to I/O priority inversion. Second, multiple independent layers in modern storage stacks are not holistically considered by existing approaches which thereby fail to effectively prioritize I/Os throughout the I/O path. In this paper, we propose a request-centric I/O prioritization that dynamically detects and prioritizes I/Os delaying request handling at all layers in the I/O path. The proposed scheme is implemented on Linux and is evaluated with three applications, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Redis. The evaluation results show that our scheme achieves up to 53% better request throughput and 42× better 99th percentile request latency (84 ms vs. 3581 ms), compared to the default configuration in Linux.

figures.caption: Application performance represented as operations per second is highly fluctuated with the CFQ, the default I/O scheduler in Linux, mainly due to the contention incurred by periodic checkpointing (60 seconds by default).
